objectives.description: You come to against the tunnel wall, pockets intact, pride collected as toll. The chain waits.
The Toll-Cutter unhooks the chain and waves you past like an old debt. In the tunnels, beating the toll IS the toll.
A grate above your head opens on the Concord hall's floor. Through it: the great table's underside, and carved there, hidden from every chair, one word in an old hand. You cannot quite read it.
The dark trades in what the light forgets. Three caches of it are open to you.
The Toll-Cutter's ledger lists tonight's traffic: five houses' worth of goods moving down, and one house's worth moving up.
One kiln has been cold for decades yet swept clean this week. Somebody tends a dead fire down here.
The old smugglers show you a sign scratched at three junctions: the same mark as under the table. They call it 'the gardener's knot'.
Before dawn the tunnels collect. One favor per head, and three houses have posted theirs at the junction stone.

The Exchequer of the Brassmark receives you in the debt vault, where the wall of lockboxes has one hole punched through it. 'Someone has withdrawn against the peace,' she says. 'The Vaultguard will not let even me pass until the floor is settled. Settle it.'
The Brassmark Vaultguard sets its feet on the counting floor. The floor gets settled.
objectives.drawDescription: The battle ended in a draw
objectives.failDescription: You failed to defeat the opponent

objectives.description: The Vaultguard racks you like a mis-shelved ledger. The Exchequer watches without expression. The floor remains unsettled.

The Vaultguard yields the floor. The Exchequer walks the breach with a lamp and does arithmetic aloud, softly, the way other people pray. 'Nothing of ours is missing,' she concludes, which appears to frighten her more than theft.

'The box that was opened is not on our books.' She closes the ledger. 'It was old when the vault was built around it. Whoever emptied it knew the peace's accounts better than the house that keeps them.' She pays you without meeting your eyes.
The Brassmark stamps your service into brass. Collection stood, floor settled, and one very old account now runs open in the dark. The house pays what it owes.

The Spindle of the Red Loom finds you without appearing to move. Her blind eyes settle just past your shoulder. 'Three of my weavers carry my thread tonight. One of them carries it to another house. Watch them. Then tell me which of my children lies.'

You watch. The tall weaver laughs too loudly at an Ironbrood joke. The young one drinks nothing all night. The gray one mends a Brassmark cuff, unasked, with red thread. The Spindle's hand finds your arm. 'Name the lie.'

nextObjectiveId.text: The young one, who will not drink
The gray one, who mends the wrong house

objectives.description: 'Laughter is loyalty renting a bigger room,' the Spindle says. 'The tall one is merely happy, which is its own small treason, but not mine to punish. Watch again.'
'The young one is with child and telling no one,' the Spindle says, gently. 'Sobriety is not conspiracy. You are reading the thread, not the weave. Watch again.'

'The gray one,' the Spindle agrees, before you finish. 'Mending is how she counts what she means to keep.' She does not raise her voice; the gray weaver simply stops existing in the room, escorted by nothing visible. 'The Loom mends too.'

'She will weave in a smaller room for a while.' The Spindle winds red thread around your wrist once and takes it back, and somehow that was the payment ceremony. The Loom owes you a favor, which is a dangerous thing to be owed.

The Provost of the Charnel Guild waits in the under-halls with an apron of blades and the patience of stone. 'A kiln down here went cold forty years ago and was never swept until this week. I want what is still in it. Bring me the salvage, and do not let anyone convince you it is theirs.'
Sweep the cold kiln and sack what the decades left: bone char, slag, and one thing that does not rattle like either.

A digger crew arrives with spades and a rehearsed grievance: the kiln is theirs, the salvage is theirs, and your sack is a misunderstanding they intend to correct. Their foreman is already rolling up his sleeves.
The digger cell closes in around the cold kiln. The misunderstanding gets corrected.
objectives.drawDescription: The battle ended in a draw
objectives.failDescription: You failed to defeat the opponent

objectives.description: The diggers take the sack and your dignity, then lose interest in both. The kiln waits, patient as its keeper.

The Provost inspects the salvage one piece at a time, then stops at the thing that does not rattle: a seal matrix, cold-cracked, its face worn smooth. 'This pressed one seal in five colors, once,' she says. 'It has not been warm in forty years. Until this week.'

'Someone tending a dead fire.' The Provost pays in bone-white without haggling, which the Guild does only when it intends to buy from you again. The under-halls know your name now, and down here that is currency.

The First of the Brood meets you at the pit rail, arms crossed, ember-scarred. 'The Brood does not do favors. The Brood does debts. Beat my champion in the circle and the debt is mine to you, witnessed. Lose, and you owe me the story of why you thought you wouldn't.'
The Ironbrood Pit Champion swings the challenge chain up onto one shoulder. The circle closes.
objectives.drawDescription: The battle ended in a draw
objectives.failDescription: You failed to defeat the opponent

objectives.description: The Champion helps you over the rail with something near courtesy. The First says nothing, which is the Brood's way of saying 'again'.

The Champion yields the circle with a bloody, genuine grin. The First vaults the rail and grips your forearm to the bone. 'Witnessed,' she says, and the whole pit repeats it, one word, like a hammer falling. 'The Brood pays its debts.'

nextObjectiveId.text: Ask why the pit stores doubled

objectives.description: The First's grin cools a degree. 'Because someone has been buying challenge rights for a fight they have not named. Paid in coin nobody at that table upstairs has minted in forty years.' She looks up through the smoke, toward the hall. 'Old money is moving.'
The First presses the iron into your palm still warm from her hand, chain-marked, debt-marked. Whatever comes for the peace, the Brood now owes you a place at their side of it.

The Grafter of the Quiet Orchard tends a potted cutting in an alcove as if the treaty were happening to other people. 'A cup must reach the Concord Table before the toast,' she says, producing it: plain pewter, faintly green within. 'Untasted, unseen, unasked about. The route is yours to choose. Choose like a gardener.'

Three routes to the table: straight across the open floor, where everyone can see there is nothing to hide. Along the servers' wall, where a cup among cups is invisible. Or through the musicians' stand, where all eyes are on hands, and no one's hands are yours.

A steward intercepts you with professional grace, relieves you of the cup 'for tasting', and returns it an hour too late. The Grafter takes it back without reproach. 'A bold graft dies of attention,' she says. 'Again.'

The cup passes down the servers' wall inside a forest of identical cups and arrives at the table unremarked. The Grafter appears beside the empty sixth chair to receive it, and sets it there, in front of no one. She catches you watching and does not explain.

'An old friend of the garden, if she comes.' The Grafter folds a jade signet into your hand like a seed into soil. 'The Orchard remembers who carries water.' The cup waits at the empty chair all night. In the morning, it is empty too.

objectives.description:
The merchant is out of breath and out of patience.

"She has my pouch, they say. The goat..
Don't let the horns fool you, she is faster than she looks. She was last seen by the market."
Search the market for the runaway goat.
Follow the trail of chewed fence line out the gate and into the open fields.
Corner the goat in the fields beyond the wall and recover the chewed coin pouch.
The goat surrenders the pouch with no visible remorse. The merchant counts it twice, then thanks you twice.
